questions.question: What is a white-collar crime?
questions.solution_html:
• White-collar crime refers to nonviolent, financially motivated offenses that are typically committed by individuals
  • businesses, or government officials in positions of trust or authority. The term was first coined by sociologist Edwin
  • Sutherland in 1939 to describe crimes committed by a person of respectability and high soci al status in the course
  • of their occupation. Common examples include: fraud (securities, mortgage, healthcare, credit card, etc.)
  • embezzlement, insider trading, bribery and corruption, money laundering, tax evasion, identity theft, cybercrime
  • and Ponzi or pyramid schemes.

questions.question: What are cognitive assessments in forensic psychology?
questions.solution_html:
• Cognitive assessment in forensic psychology evaluates a person’s mental abilities like memory, attention and
  • problem-solving, using standardized tests to help inform legal decisions. This can determine an individual’s
  • competency to stand trial, assess the impact of brain injury on behavior and evaluate the credibility of witness
  • testimony. Assessments may also explore how cognitive processes contribute to o ffending behavior.
  • Seal, Stamp, and Impression Analysis

questions.question: Which branch deals with poisons and drugs in the body?
questions.solution_html:
• The branch of forensic science that deals with poisons and drugs in the body is known as forensic toxicology. This fi
  • eld focuses on the detection and analysis of toxic substances, drugs, and poisons in biological samples, such as bloo
  • d, urine, and tissues. Forensic toxicologists play a crucial role in criminal investigations, workplace drug testing, and
  • medical examinations, helping to establish the cause of death, determine drug involvement in criminal cases, and
  • assess the impact of substances on behavior.

questions.question: What types of compensation are available for victims of crime?
questions.solution_html:
• Court-ordered compensation under Section 357 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC) requires offenders to pay
  • fines or damages to victims. State Victim Compensation Schemes under Section 357A provide financial aid to victims
  • and their dependents. The Central Victim Compensation F und (CVCF) assists states in providing compensation for
  • serious crimes such as rape, acid attacks, and human trafficking. Some states also provide interim relief for
  • immediate medical or financial needs. Furthermore, the Supreme Court and High Courts can award compensation
  • for violations of fundamental rights under Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution. (Any four valid points: 5 marks)

questions.question: Differentiate between modus operandi & signature in concept with forensic behavioral analysis.
questions.solution_html:
• The modus operandi (MO) refers to the method of operation, the techniques and procedures a criminal consistently
  • uses to commit crimes. In contrast, a signature involves behaviors or details of the crime that are not necessary to
  • accomplish it but fulfill the offender’s psyc hological or emotional needs (for instance, specific ritualistic actions
  • posing of the body, or leaving a particular mark or object at the scene). Unlike the modus operandi, the signature
  • tends to remain more fixed because it stems from the offender’s inn er fantasies or personality, and thus it can be a
  • powerful clue in linking crimes to the same individual. (Correct answer: 5 marks)

questions.question: Name any three characteristics of forensic science.
questions.solution_html:
• Forensic Science is the scientific discipline engaged in the recognition, identification, individualization, and
  • evaluation of physical evidence by using the laws and principles of natural science to find answers to doubtful
  • questions that may arise in a court of law. It encompasses various scientific disciplines an d integrates them to
  • support investigations, legal proceedings, and the administration of justice. The range of a forensics includes either
  • one or all the three following major activities in analyzing and interpreting the physical evidences in the forensic
  • science laboratories: Identification, Individualization & Reconstruction

questions.question: What does the DNA Fingerprinting Unit in State FSLs specialize in?
questions.solution_html:
• State FSLs in India specialize in using DNA fingerprinting to generate DNA profiles from various biological exhibits
  • and compare them to link suspects to crime scenes, identify victims and resolve disputed relationships. State FSLs
  • use DNA Analysis for a range of critical cases such as
  • Violent crimes like murder, se xual assault, rape , Paternity and Maternity disputes , Identification of unidentified
  • bodies, Mass disasters, Child trafficking, Identification from trace evidence, Wildlife crimes

questions.question: Explain the major functions and duties of Government Examiner of Questioned Documents (GEQD).
questions.solution_html:
• The Government Examiner of Questioned Documents (GEQD) is a highly specialized forensic a uthority in India
  • responsible for the scientific examination of documentary evidence. GEQD laboratories function under the
  • Directorate of Forensic Science Services (DFSS), Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India. Their findings
  • support law -enforcement agencies and judicial authorities in resolving disputes related to written and printed
  • materials.
